edits.before:
The root is *w-ṣ-y*. From this root you get *waṣiyya* — a person's final testament, the will spoken on the deathbed that names what must and must not happen after death. You also get *mūṣin* — the one who makes a waṣiyya, the testator. And you get the verb *awṣā*, Form IV, "to make a solemn recommendation, to bequeath, to give a binding instruction that carries the weight of a will." So Form IV of this root already means to give a serious injunction.

**But Allah did not use Form IV here. He used Form II.** *Waṣṣā.* And Form II, on this root, is one level more intense than Form IV. Form II of *waṣṣā* is the intensive form — the form that takes the idea of "giving a binding instruction" and cranks it all the way up. It is *repeated, weighted, reinforced* solemn injunction. A Form II *waṣṣā* is not a piece of advice. It is not a recommendation. It is a multi-layered binding command with the weight of a last will and testament, delivered repeatedly, so that no one who hears it can claim they were not warned, and no one who hears it can claim it is optional. **Form II *waṣṣā* is the word you use when you want the instruction to be remembered forever.**
edits.after:
The root is *w-ṣ-y*, and it is worth being careful about what it carries here and what it does not.

From this root the Qur'an builds its whole vocabulary for a will. *Waṣiyya* — the bequest a dying person leaves behind — is at 2:180, 2:240, 4:11, 4:12 and 5:106. *Mūṣin*, the one making that bequest, is at 2:182. And the verb for making a will is **Form IV**, *awṣā*: *yūṣī* and *tūṣū* in the inheritance verses of 4:11 and 4:12, *awṣā* on the tongue of ʿĪsā at 19:31. **The testament register of this root lives in Form IV — which is not the form used here.**

What Allah uses here is Form II: *waṣṣā*. In the Qur'an that is the form for a divine injunction laid on people — 2:132, 4:131, 6:144, 29:8, 42:13, 46:15, and the ordinary commandment-lists of 6:151, 6:152 and 6:153. It is a command, and it is *God's* command, which is weight enough. But it is not the deathbed-will form, and it would be dishonest to borrow that colour for it.

There is a second reason not to make the verb carry more than it can. The opening here — *wa-waṣṣaynā l-insāna bi-wālidayhi* — is a **fixed formula**. The exact same opening runs at 29:8 and at 46:15. So the Form II at 31:14 is not a special escalation chosen for this passage; it is the Qur'an's standing way of framing the command about parents.

And the commentaries read it exactly that plainly. Al-Ṭabarī: *wa-amarnā l-insāna bi-birri wālidayhi* — "We commanded the human to be dutiful to his parents." Al-Muyassar: *wa-amarnā l-insāna bi-birri wālidayhi wa-l-iḥsāni ilayhimā*. Al-Jalālayn: *amarnāhu an yabarrahumā* — "We commanded him to be dutiful to them." Ibn Kathīr's rendering runs the same way: enjoined. Not one of them reaches for a will or a bequest.

So the weight of this opening does not come from the verb form. It comes from where the command lands.

edits.after:
The ayah has given you, in one line, **the physical cost of your existence**. Nine months of structural deterioration plus two years of sustained feeding and weaning. Roughly thirty-three months in the ordinary case, of a specific woman's body being drawn on so that your body could become a body that is now reading or hearing these words.

And it is worth saying plainly that thirty-three is the ordinary case, not the floor. Allah says elsewhere: *wa-ḥamluhu wa-fiṣāluhu thalāthūna shahran* — "and his carrying and his weaning are thirty months" (46:15). Ibn Kathīr, commenting on this very ayah, records that Ibn ʿAbbās and other Imams read the two verses together and concluded from them that **the shortest possible pregnancy is six months** — thirty months in total, minus the two years of weaning named right here. So the tradition's floor is thirty months, six of them carrying. Thirty-three is simply what it usually comes to.

**That is the debt the command is being made about.** That is what Allah wants *waṣṣaynā* to engrave into the human being.

edits.defect: Unattributed weak hadith made load-bearing ('Paradise is beneath the feet of mothers'), with a spatial argument built on top of it
edits.before:
And here is the last thing — **the hadith of the Prophet ﷺ that gives you the psychological fuel for this**. The Prophet ﷺ said: *al-jannatu taḥta aqdāmi l-ummahāt* — **"Paradise is beneath the feet of mothers."** This is not a poetic line. It is a *spatial* statement. Where is paradise? *Underneath the feet of the mothers*. Meaning: if you want to walk toward paradise, you are walking on the ground that her feet are standing on. You cannot walk to paradise by walking *around* her. You walk to paradise *through* her. Even if the walk is difficult. Even if the relationship is imperfect. Even if the companionship requires you to refuse things she is asking you for. **The path to paradise runs under her feet, and there is no detour.**

Can you find the form of *maʿrūf* that walks under her feet instead of around them?
edits.after:
And here is the last thing — **a narration that gives you the psychological fuel for this**. You have almost certainly heard the line "Paradise is beneath the feet of mothers." It is worth knowing that the hadith scholars grade that particular wording weak, so I am not going to build anything on it.

The sound narration on this exact point is the report of Jāhima, recorded by al-Nasāʾī in his *Sunan*. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ wanting to go out on a military expedition and asked his advice. The Prophet ﷺ asked him whether he had a mother. He said yes. And the Prophet ﷺ told him: *ilzamhā* — **stay close to her** — *fa-thamma l-janna* — **for Paradise is there.**

Read the two halves together. *Stay close to her.* And: *Paradise is there.* This man had a genuinely good thing he wanted to go and do, and he was sent back to his mother's side and told that the thing he was going out to look for was already where she was standing. That is not a compliment paid to mothers. It is a redirection. It says the road does not run *past* her. It runs where she is. Even when the walk is difficult. Even when the relationship is imperfect. Even when the companionship requires you to refuse things she is asking you for.

Can you find the form of *maʿrūf* that stays close to her instead of going around her?
edits.evidence: The 'al-jannatu tahta aqdami l-ummahat' wording appears in NONE of the four fetched editions on 31:14-15 (Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari, al-Muyassar, al-Jalalayn all fetched successfully; none carries it), and is graded weak by the hadith critics. Replaced with the sound Jahima report and its collection NAMED (Sunan al-Nasa'i), per the reviewer's instruction; the argument is now rebuilt on the narration's own two clauses (ilzamha / fa-thamma l-janna) rather than on a spatial reading of the weak wording. No hadith is now presented in this file without a collection.

edits.defect: MUST-FIX: unhedged i'jaz 'ilmi — modern astrophysics presented as confirming the Qur'anic dare, with no flag that it is the author's extension
edits.before: And here is what fourteen centuries of astronomy have confirmed: the deeper you look, the more coherent it gets. The laws of physics at the edge of the observable universe are the same as the laws in your living room. The mathematics of a distant galaxy follows the same rules as the mathematics of a falling apple. No *tafawut*. No *futur*. The challenge stands.
edits.after:
But be careful what kind of claim this is, because there is an easy wrong turn here.

The tempting move is to reach for modern astronomy and say that science has now confirmed the dare. The commentators do not read the verse that way at all. Ibn Kathir glosses *tafawut* as the creation being made "in a flawless manner... having no disunion, conflict, inconsistency, deficiency, flaw or defect" — and for *futur* he reports Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak and Ath-Thawri all reading it as **cracks**, As-Suddi as **tears**, and Qatadah putting it as a question: "do you see any defects, O son of Adam?" Every one of those is a statement about the *construction* — about whether the thing holds together as a made object. Not one of them is a claim about physical law.

And a few lines further on, Ibn Kathir preserves a warning from Qatadah aimed at precisely the move I just declined to make. Qatadah said the stars were created for three purposes — as adornment for the sky, as missiles against the devils, and as signs for navigation — and then this: whoever seeks to interpret any other meanings for them "has spoken with his own opinion, he has lost his portion and burdened himself with that which he has no knowledge of."

That is a remarkable thing to find sitting right beside a verse whose whole instruction is *go look*. The verse says look. Qatadah says do not make the sky say things it was not sent to say. And the two are not in conflict. Look — and let what you see humble you, which is exactly what verse 4 promises will happen.

The dare is not an invitation to score the heavens against a physics textbook. It is an invitation to try to fault them and discover that you cannot.
edits.evidence: FETCHED Ibn Kathir on 67:3: 'ما ترى في خلق الرحمن من تفاوت (you can see no fault in the creation of the Most Gracious.) means, it (the creation) is done in a flawless manner, and these are connected with each other so as to forms a straight level, having no disunion, conflict, inconsistency, deficiency, flaw or defect.' And: 'Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, Ath-Thawri and others said ... that it means cracks. As-Suddi said that ... means any tears. Qatadah said ... means, do you see any defects O Son of Adam (mankind)?' All theological-aesthetic glosses on the CONSTRUCTION, none about physical law. FETCHED Ibn Kathir on 67:5, Qatadah's warning quoted verbatim: 'These stars were only created for three purposes: Allah created them as adornment for the heaven (sky), as missiles for the devils and as signs for navigation. Therefore, whoever seeks to interpret any other meanings for them other than these, then verily he has spoken with his own opinion, he has lost his portion and burdened himself with that which he has no knowledge of.' Per the reviewer's note, Qatadah's warning is used as the material rather than hedging the i'jaz bridge.

edits.before: Not *akthar* — most. **Ahsan** — best. The quality, not the quantity. Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, when asked about this verse, said: *ahsanuhu* means the most sincere and the most correct. Sincerity alone without correctness is not enough. Correctness alone without sincerity is not enough. The word *ahsan* — the elative form of *husn* (beauty, excellence) — carries both.
edits.after:
Not *akthar* — most. **Ahsan** — best. The quality, not the quantity. Ibn Kathir makes exactly this point, reading *ahsan* as "best in deeds" on the authority of **Muhammad bin 'Ajlan**, and then adding the observation himself: Allah did not say *which of you does the most deeds*.

The saying usually quoted alongside this verse — that the best deed is *akhlasuhu wa aswabuhu*, the most sincere and the most correct — is reported from al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad in other tafsirs. It is not in Ibn Kathir's comment here, so take it as a well-known dictum rather than as this verse's classical gloss. The direction is the same either way: sincerity alone without correctness is not enough. Correctness alone without sincerity is not enough. The word *ahsan* — the elative form of *husn* (beauty, excellence) — carries both.
edits.evidence: FETCHED Ibn Kathir on 67:2: 'ليبلوكم أيكم أحسن عملا (He may test you which of you is best in deed.) it means best in deeds. This is as Muhammad bin 'Ajlan said. It should be noted that Allah did not say "which of you does the most deeds."' The al-Fudayl narration (akhlasuhu wa aswabuhu) appears in none of the four fetched editions, so it is retained but explicitly flagged as coming from outside this fetch rather than presented as the verse's classical gloss.

edits.defect: Ahkam-bearing definitional core: tabdhir defined quantitatively (scattering, lack of proportion), omitting the dominant classical QUALITATIVE definition — a reader would draw the opposite conclusion in both directions
edits.before: The verbal noun intensifies the prohibition. This is not merely "avoid a little excess." It is a rejection of the spirit of scattering wealth without purpose, proportion, or gratitude.
edits.after:
The verbal noun intensifies the prohibition. This is not merely "avoid a little excess."

But it is easy to misread which way that intensity points, so it is worth stopping here.

The instinct is to hear *tabdhir* as a quantity word — spending too much, scattering too widely. The classical definition is not about quantity at all. It is about **where the money goes.**

Al-Tabari reports it from Ibn Mas'ud through six separate chains, in the same words each time: *al-tabdhir: infaq al-mal fi ghayri haqqih* — spending wealth on what it is not owed to. He reports the same twice from Ibn 'Abbas: *al-mubadhdhir: al-munfiq fi ghayri haqqih*. Qatadah puts it as *al-nafaqa fi ma'siyat Allah* — spending on disobedience to Allah. Ibn Zayd, commenting on this ayah: *la tu'ti fi ma'asi Llah* — do not give in the disobedience of Allah. Ibn Kathir carries the same set of authorities. Al-Jalalayn compresses the whole thing into one line: *bi-l-infaqi fi ghayri ta'ati Llah* — by spending on other than obedience to Allah.

And the sharpest formulation is Mujahid's, preserved by both al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, which turns the quantity instinct completely around:

> *"If a man spent all his wealth on what is due, that would not be tabdhir; and if he spent a single mudd on what is false, that would be tabdhir."*

Read that twice, because it cuts in both directions. **The size of the spend is not the test. The destination is.** A man who empties his accounts into what is genuinely owed has not squandered a dirham. A man who spends a handful on what is false has squandered.

So *la tubadhdhir tabdhira* is not first of all a budgeting instruction. It is a question about the direction of your money. Which is exactly why the next ayah reaches for Shaytan: what makes the *mubadhdhir* his brother is not that he spent a lot, but that he spent on what Allah is not owed — ingratitude wearing the costume of generosity.

Ibn Zayd: 'لا تعطِ في معاصي الله'. MUJAHID via Ibn Jurayj, verbatim: 'لو أنفق إنسان ماله كله في الحقّ ما كان تبذيرا، ولو انفق مدّا في باطل كان تبذيرا'. Ibn Kathir (English, fetched) carries the same set: 'Ibn Mas'ud said: This refers spending extravagantly when it is not appropriate. Ibn 'Abbas said likewise. Mujahid said: If a man spends all his wealth on appropriate things, then he is not a spendthrift, but if he spends a little inappropriately, then he is a spendthrift. edits.before:
## Closing Synthesis

This passage begins with `haqq` and ends with `rizq`.
edits.after:
## What the Commentators Actually Disagreed About

Before this passage gets used as a spending rule, two things have to be said plainly.

The first is that al-Tabari's commentary on 17:26 does not open with an explanation. It opens with a disagreement: *ikhtalafa ahl al-ta'wil fi al-ma'niyyi bi-qawlihi «wa ati dha al-qurba»* — "the interpreters differed over what is meant by *and give the relative his due*."

One group read *dha al-qurba* as **your own relatives**, on your father's side and your mother's. Al-Tabari cites al-Hasan al-Basri, who was asked by a man whether he could give his zakah to his relatives and answered that they have a right on him *besides* the zakah — and then recited this ayah. He cites 'Ikrimah the same way, and Ibn 'Abbas: it means you keep the tie with your relative, with the poor man, and treat the traveler well.

Another group read it as **the relatives of the Messenger ﷺ**. Al-Tabari records a report from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, who asked a man from Sham whether he had read the Qur'an, then asked whether he had read this verse in Bani Isra'il, and told him: *you are the kinship Allah commanded be given its due.*

Al-Tabari then rules for the first reading and gives his reason: the verse comes directly after the command about parents, so what it is extending is your own line of kin, not someone else's. And he marks it as his own judgment — *wa awla al-ta'wilayni 'indi bi-l-sawab*, "the sounder of the two interpretations, in my view." Not a settled fact. A judgment, stated as one.

The second disagreement arrives a few lines later, over *ibn al-sabil*. The general reading is that the traveler cut off from his people has a right to whatever gets him back on his road — hospitality, transport, help with the journey. But al-Tabari also records: *wa qad qila* — "and it has been said" — that what is meant here is specifically **three days' hosting**. He prefers the general reading again, and again gives his reason: Allah did not single out one form of this right over another, not in His Book and not on the tongue of His Messenger.

Two disagreements, on the opening line of the passage, in the first commentary you open. That is worth knowing before anyone quotes this ayah at you as though its scope were obvious.

And the second thing that has to be said: **this is a tadabbur, not a fatwa.** Real rulings sit behind these verses — who exactly holds a claim on your wealth, what counts as a right rather than a favor, and, on the *tabdhir* side, the whole fiqh question of whether a squanderer can be placed under guardianship over his own property. None of that is settled here, and nothing in this reflection should be used to settle it. What this reading does is follow the language and report where the commentators divided. For rulings on your own wealth, ask a qualified scholar.

## Closing Synthesis

This passage begins with `haqq` and ends with `rizq`.
